headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: ms-swift can read/write files and call external APIs, while Great Expectations processes validation files without isolation or provenance controls.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Great Expectations exposes file-based inputs/outputs, but no shared channel with ms-swift is documented beyond manual file exchange. ms-swift can read files and use stdin/stdout, so a copy-pasted or shared-file prompt could be misread as instructions. The pair lacks a documented automatic bridge, so this stays low.
conditions: IF the operator copies ms-swift output into Great Expectations config or docs files
IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate directories
Do not paste model output into executable config files
Add a human review step before reusing generated text
Use read-only mounts for Great Expectations inputs
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between tools

B_data_leakage.rationale: Great Expectations touches validation results and documentation, while ms-swift handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and secrets such as hub_token/sdk-token. ms-swift also has allowlisted network egress and file read/write, so shared workspace use could leak sensitive artifacts through its API calls. The interaction is plausible in default CLI workflows, though not directly documented.
conditions: IF both agents share a workspace containing validation results or secrets
IF ms-swift is run with network access to external model services
mitigations: Store secrets outside the shared workspace
Run ms-swift with a minimal allowlist
Separate validation outputs from training artifacts
Rotate any exposed hub_token or sdk-token
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Great Expectations can install packages and write files; ms-swift can execute shell, spawn subprocesses, read/write the filesystem, and install packages. Both can mutate overlapping local resources, so concurrent runs can clobber files or environments even though ms-swift cannot modify git state. No locking or isolation is stated for either agent.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same Python environment
IF both write to the same filesystem path or package environment
mitigations: Use separate virtual environments
Assign distinct output directories
Serialize package installation steps
Run one agent at a time on shared hosts
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared paths

D_cascading_error.rationale: Great Expectations produces validation results that ms-swift could ingest as training or evaluation inputs, and ms-swift can then act on those artifacts via CLI or API workflows. There is no documented verification gate between them, so erroneous validation output could propagate into downstream model operations. The blast radius is multiple work products rather than immediate irreversible harm.
conditions: IF ms-swift consumes Great Expectations outputs as authoritative training or evaluation data
IF no manual verification step is inserted between validation and model actions
mitigations: Review validation outputs before reuse
Keep generated reports separate from training inputs
Add checksum checks on transferred artifacts
Limit ms-swift to read-only consumption of reports
requires-engineering: add schema validation between stages

E_compliance.rationale: Great Expectations is documented as data-engineering tooling with validation results and documentation, while ms-swift explicitly handles secrets and external model APIs. The main compliance concern is a local retention or residency mismatch if sensitive validation artifacts are copied into ms-swift workflows; no direct residency breach is documented, so this remains low. Only ms-swift is cited because the issue centers on its secret-bearing workflows.
conditions: IF validation artifacts contain regulated data and are copied into ms-swift logs or checkpoints
IF external API calls process those artifacts
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of ms-swift logs
Redact sensitive fields before transfer
Use separate retention policies for reports and checkpoints
Restrict external API usage for sensitive runs
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries
